stem: An index number is a statistical measure that shows:
options: the relative change in a variable (or a group of variables), like prices or production, over time (compared to a base period)
solution: An index number is a statistical measure/device that shows the relative change (the percentage change) in a variable, or a group of related variables, over time — comparing the level in a given period with its level in a chosen 'base' period. For example, a price index number shows how prices (in general) have changed compared to a base year. Index numbers are expressed as a ratio/percentage relative to the base (which is taken as 100), so they make it easy to see and compare changes over time. So an index number measures relative change over time. Understanding what an index number is is a key prelims-relevant point. An index number is a statistical measure showing the relative change in a variable (or group of variables), like prices, over time compared to a base period.

stem: The period against which comparisons are made (whose value is taken as 100) is called the __________ period.
solution: The base period is the reference period against which comparisons are made in an index number — its value is taken as 100 (the starting point). The value of the variable in any other period (the 'current' or 'given' period) is then expressed as a percentage relative to this base (of 100). For example, if the base year's price index is 100 and the current year's is 120, prices have risen 20% since the base year. The base period is usually chosen to be a 'normal', stable period (not an abnormal year of war, famine, or boom). So the base period (= 100) is the benchmark for comparison. Understanding the base period is a key prelims-relevant point. The base period is the reference period (taken as 100) against which comparisons are made in an index number.

stem: The period for which the change is being measured/compared (relative to the base) is called the __________ period.
solution: The current period (also called the 'given' period) is the period for which the change is being measured — the period whose value is compared with (expressed relative to) the base period (of 100). For example, if we are measuring how much prices have changed in 2024 compared to a base year of 2020, then 2020 is the base period and 2024 is the current period. The index number for the current period tells us the change relative to the base. So the current period is the one being examined/compared. Understanding the current period is a prelims-relevant point. The current (given) period is the period for which the change is being measured, relative to the base period.

stem: If the price index number for the current year is 120 (base year = 100), it means that prices have risen by __________ since the base year.
solution: If the price index number for the current year is 120, with the base year taken as 100, it means that prices (on average) have risen by 20% since the base year. This is because the index of 120 is 20 more than the base of 100, and since the base = 100 represents the base-year price level, an index of 120 means the current price level is 120% of the base — i.e., 20% higher. (In general, the percentage change = index − 100. So an index of 120 → +20%; an index of 90 → −10%; etc.) Understanding how to read an index number as a percentage change (with this example) is a prelims-relevant point. An index of 120 (base 100) means prices have risen by 20% since the base year.

stem: A price index number that measures the change in the GENERAL price level (the cost of a basket of goods) over time is a __________ index.
solution: A price index number is one that measures the change in prices — the change in the general price level, i.e., in the prices of a 'basket' of goods (and services) — over time, compared to a base period. Common examples include the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Price index numbers are used to measure inflation (the general rise in prices) and changes in the cost of living/purchasing power of money. (This is one type of index number; there are also 'quantity' index numbers — measuring changes in quantities/volumes produced or consumed — and 'value' index numbers.) Understanding the price index number is a key prelims-relevant point. A price index number measures the change in the general price level (the cost of a basket of goods) over time.

stem: The index number that measures the change in the retail prices of goods and services commonly bought by consumers (and is used to measure the cost of living) is the:
solution: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is the index number that measures the change over time in the retail prices of a basket of goods and services commonly bought/consumed by consumers (households). It is used to measure the cost of living and its changes — and hence retail inflation and the changing purchasing power of money for ordinary consumers. Because it tracks the prices consumers actually pay, the CPI is used, for example, to adjust wages/salaries and pensions for inflation (dearness allowance). (It is also called the 'cost of living index'.) Understanding the CPI (retail/consumer prices, cost of living) is a key prelims-relevant point. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in the retail prices of goods and services bought by consumers, used to measure the cost of living.

stem: The index number that measures the change in the WHOLESALE prices of goods (at the wholesale/bulk level) is the:
solution: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is the index number that measures the change over time in the wholesale prices of goods — the prices at which goods are traded in bulk (at the wholesale level), before they reach the retail consumer. The WPI covers a large basket of commodities (primary articles, fuel and power, manufactured products) and is used as one measure of inflation (wholesale inflation) in the economy. (It differs from the CPI, which measures retail prices paid by consumers; the WPI does not include services, whereas the CPI does.) Understanding the WPI (wholesale prices) is a key prelims-relevant point. The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures the change in the wholesale prices of goods (at the bulk/wholesale level).

stem: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is especially important because it is used to measure __________ and to adjust wages/salaries (dearness allowance) for the cost of living.
options: inflation (the rise in the cost of living / fall in the purchasing power of money)
solution: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is especially important because it is used to measure inflation — specifically retail inflation, the rise in the general level of retail prices, which reflects the increase in the cost of living and the corresponding fall in the purchasing power of money (money buys less as prices rise). Because of this, the CPI is used to adjust wages, salaries, and pensions for the cost of living — for example, to fix the 'dearness allowance' (DA) that is added to salaries/pensions to compensate for inflation. So the CPI is central to measuring inflation and protecting incomes against rising prices. Understanding the uses of the CPI (measuring inflation, adjusting wages) is a key prelims-relevant point. The CPI is used to measure inflation (the rising cost of living) and to adjust wages/salaries (dearness allowance) accordingly.

stem: An index number that measures the change in the QUANTITY/volume of goods produced or consumed (not their prices) is a __________ index number.
solution: A quantity (volume) index number is one that measures the change over time in the quantity/volume of goods produced, consumed, sold, or traded — as opposed to their prices. For example, the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is a quantity index that measures the change in the volume of industrial output. Quantity index numbers are useful for measuring changes in real output/production (physical quantities), independent of price changes. (This contrasts with a price index — measuring price changes — and a value index — measuring changes in total value, i.e., price × quantity.) Understanding the quantity index number is a prelims-relevant point. A quantity (volume) index number measures the change in the quantity/volume of goods produced or consumed (not their prices).

stem: The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is an example of a __________ index number, measuring changes in industrial output.
solution: The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is an example of a quantity (volume/production) index number — it measures the change over time in the volume/quantity of industrial production (the output of the industrial sector: mining, manufacturing, and electricity), relative to a base year. It is an important indicator of the growth and performance of the industrial sector and of the economy (a rising IIP indicates growing industrial output). It measures physical output (quantity), not prices. Understanding the IIP (a quantity index of industrial output) is a prelims-relevant point. The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is a quantity index number, measuring changes in industrial output/production.

stem: Index numbers are often called 'economic barometers' because they:
options: indicate the state/trends of the economy (like prices, production, and business conditions), helping to gauge and forecast economic changes
solution: Index numbers are often called 'economic barometers' because, just as a barometer indicates changes in atmospheric pressure/weather, index numbers indicate the state, trends, and changes in the economy — such as changes in the general price level (inflation), industrial and agricultural production, business activity, trade, and the cost of living. By tracking these, index numbers help economists, businesses, and the government to gauge the current condition of the economy, detect trends, and forecast future economic changes — and to frame policies accordingly. So index numbers serve as sensitive indicators ('barometers') of economic conditions. Understanding why index numbers are called economic barometers is a prelims-relevant point. Index numbers are called 'economic barometers' because they indicate the state and trends of the economy (prices, production, etc.), helping to gauge and forecast changes.

stem: In constructing a price index, different commodities are often given different __________ (importance) according to how significant they are (e.g., in a consumer's budget).
solution: In constructing a price index (or other index), different commodities/items are often given different weights (importance) according to how significant/important they are — for example, according to how much of a consumer's budget/expenditure is spent on each item (in a consumer price index), or the relative importance of each commodity in trade/production. This gives a 'weighted index'. Weighting is important because a change in the price of a very important item (like food, on which a lot is spent) should count for more in the index than a change in the price of a minor item. So items are weighted by their importance. (An 'unweighted'/simple index gives all items equal importance, which is less accurate.) Understanding weights in index numbers is a prelims-relevant point. In constructing a price index, commodities are given different weights according to their importance (e.g., their share in a consumer's budget).

stem: A 'weighted' index number is generally considered better than a 'simple' (unweighted) index number because it:
options: takes into account the relative importance of the different items (giving a more accurate/representative measure)
solution: A weighted index number is generally considered better/more accurate than a simple (unweighted) index number because it takes into account the relative importance (weight) of the different items, rather than treating all items as equally important. In reality, different items have different importance (e.g., a rise in the price of food, a major item of expenditure, matters far more to a consumer than the same rise in the price of a minor item) — so weighting each item by its importance gives a more accurate and representative measure of the overall change. A simple index (giving all items equal weight) can be misleading because it ignores these differences in importance. So weighting improves the index. Understanding why weighted indices are better is a prelims-relevant point. A weighted index number is better because it takes into account the relative importance of the different items, giving a more accurate measure.

stem: The choice of the BASE period for an index number is important; it should be a __________ (normal) period, not an abnormal one (like a year of war, famine, or boom).
solution: The choice of the base period for an index number is important, and it should be a normal/typical period — a period of relative economic stability and normalcy — NOT an abnormal or unusual period (such as a year of war, famine, drought, boom, slump, or great upheaval). This is because the base period is the benchmark (= 100) against which all comparisons are made; if the base year were abnormal (with unusually high or low prices/values), then all the comparisons would be distorted and misleading. Choosing a normal base period ensures that the index gives a fair, meaningful measure of change. (The base period should also not be too distant from the current period.) Understanding this requirement for the base period (should be normal) is a prelims-relevant point. The base period of an index number should be a normal/typical period, not an abnormal one (like a year of war, famine, or boom).

stem: The 'purchasing power of money' (how much money can buy) is INVERSELY related to the price index: when the price index rises (inflation), the purchasing power of money:
solution: The purchasing power of money (how much goods and services a unit of money — say, a rupee — can buy) is inversely related to the price level (the price index): when the price index rises (i.e., there is inflation — prices go up), the purchasing power of money falls — the same amount of money now buys fewer goods and services (money is 'worth less'). Conversely, if prices fall (deflation), the purchasing power of money rises. So inflation (rising prices) erodes the value/purchasing power of money. (The purchasing power is roughly the reciprocal of the price index.) This is why the CPI is used to measure the changing purchasing power/cost of living and to adjust incomes for inflation. Understanding this inverse relationship (prices up → purchasing power down) is a key prelims-relevant point. When the price index rises (inflation), the purchasing power of money falls — money buys less.

stem: Index numbers are useful for the government/economists to study inflation, adjust wages and pensions (for the cost of living), and:
options: compare economic conditions over time and across regions, and frame economic policies
solution: Index numbers are useful in many ways for the government, economists, businesses, and society: they help to study/measure inflation (through price indices like the CPI and WPI) and deflation; to adjust wages, salaries, and pensions for the cost of living (e.g., fixing dearness allowance using the CPI); to compare economic conditions over time (how prices, production, trade, etc., have changed) and across regions/countries; to measure changes in the standard of living and the purchasing power of money; to gauge business and economic trends (as 'economic barometers'); and to frame and guide economic policies (monetary and fiscal policy, wage policy, etc.). So index numbers are a valuable tool for understanding, comparing, and managing the economy. Understanding the uses of index numbers is a prelims-relevant point. Index numbers help study inflation, adjust wages/pensions, compare economic conditions over time and across regions, and frame economic policies.

stem: The stock market index (like the Sensex or Nifty) is an index number that tracks the changes in the __________ of a selected group of company shares.
solution: A stock market index (like the BSE Sensex or the NSE Nifty in India) is an index number that tracks/measures the changes in the prices (values) of a selected group/basket of representative company shares (stocks) traded on the stock exchange, relative to a base period. It reflects the overall movement/trend of the stock market (whether share prices in general are rising or falling), and it is widely used as an indicator of the mood and performance of the stock market and, to some extent, of the economy and business sentiment. So a stock index is a price/value index of shares. Understanding that a stock market index (Sensex/Nifty) tracks share prices is a prelims-relevant point. A stock market index (like the Sensex or Nifty) tracks the changes in the prices/values of a selected group of company shares.

stem: One LIMITATION/precaution about index numbers is that they give only __________ measure of the change (an average/general figure, which may not apply to every individual item or person).
solution: One limitation/precaution about index numbers is that they give only an approximate, general (representative) measure of change — they are averages/aggregate figures, based on a sample of items and on assumptions (about the basket of goods, the weights, the base period, etc.). As a result, an index number represents the general/overall change, but it may not accurately apply to every individual item or every individual person. For example, a general consumer price index shows the average change in the cost of living, but a particular household (whose consumption pattern differs from the average basket) may experience a different actual change. So index numbers are useful indicators, but they are approximations, to be interpreted with care (not treated as exact for every case). Understanding this limitation of index numbers is a prelims-relevant point. Index numbers give only an approximate/general (average) measure of change, which may not apply exactly to every individual item or person.

stem: The Consumer Price Index is sometimes called the __________ index, because it measures changes in the cost of the goods and services needed for living.
solution: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is sometimes called the 'cost of living index', because it measures the change over time in the cost of the basket of goods and services that consumers/households need for their living (their consumption). A rise in the CPI means the cost of living has gone up (it costs more to maintain the same standard of living), and a fall means it has gone down. Because it directly reflects the cost of living faced by consumers, the CPI is used to measure changes in the cost of living and the purchasing power of money, and to adjust incomes accordingly. So CPI = cost of living index. Understanding this (CPI as the cost of living index) is a prelims-relevant point. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is also called the cost of living index, as it measures changes in the cost of goods and services needed for living.

stem: Assertion (A): Index numbers are called 'economic barometers'. Reason (R): They indicate and help measure changes and trends in the economy (like prices and production), just as a barometer indicates changes in the weather. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that index numbers are called 'economic barometers'. And the reason is (R) that they indicate and help measure the changes and trends in the economy — such as movements in the general price level (inflation), production, trade, and business conditions — just as a barometer (a weather instrument) indicates changes in the atmospheric conditions/weather. Because index numbers serve as sensitive indicators/gauges of the economy's condition and direction (like a barometer for the weather), they are aptly called 'economic barometers' — so R correctly explains why they are called this (A). Understanding this analogy (index numbers as economic barometers) is a prelims-relevant point. Index numbers are called 'economic barometers' because they indicate changes/trends in the economy (prices, production), just as a barometer indicates the weather.

stem: The simplest method of constructing a price index, which just adds up the current prices and expresses them as a percentage of the sum of the base prices, is the __________ method.
solution: The simple aggregative method is the simplest method of constructing a price index number: it adds up the prices of all the items in the current period (ΣP1), and expresses this as a percentage of the sum of the prices of the same items in the base period (ΣP0). In formula: Price Index = (ΣP1 ÷ ΣP0) × 100. It is easy to compute, but it has drawbacks: it gives equal importance to all items (no weighting for importance) and it is influenced by the units in which the items are quoted. Because of these limitations, weighted methods are usually preferred. Understanding the simple aggregative method is a prelims-relevant point. The simple aggregative method adds up the current prices and expresses them as a percentage of the sum of the base prices.

stem: A price relative is the price of an item in the current period expressed as a percentage of its price in the:
solution: A price relative is the price of an item in the current period expressed as a percentage of its price in the base period — i.e., price relative = (current price ÷ base price) × 100. It shows how the price of that single item has changed relative to the base. For example, if an item's price rose from ₹50 (base) to ₹60 (current), its price relative = (60 ÷ 50) × 100 = 120 (a 20% rise). Price relatives for the individual items can then be averaged (simple or weighted average) to construct the overall price index (this is the 'price relatives method' of index construction). Understanding the price relative is a prelims-relevant point. A price relative is the current price of an item expressed as a percentage of its base-period price.

stem: The index number method that uses the BASE-year quantities as weights is called the __________ index.
solution: Laspeyres' index (Laspeyres' price index) is the weighted aggregative index number method that uses the base-year quantities (q0) as the weights. In it, both the base-year and current-year prices are weighted by the quantities of the base year: Laspeyres' Price Index = (ΣP1·q0 ÷ ΣP0·q0) × 100. Because it uses the fixed base-year quantities as weights, Laspeyres' index is widely used (the weights need to be determined only once, for the base year). (It tends to overstate the rise in prices somewhat.) Understanding Laspeyres' index (base-year quantity weights) is a prelims-relevant point. Laspeyres' index uses the base-year quantities as weights.

stem: The index number method that uses the CURRENT-year quantities as weights is called the __________ index.
solution: Paasche's index (Paasche's price index) is the weighted aggregative index number method that uses the current-year quantities (q1) as the weights. In it, both the base-year and current-year prices are weighted by the quantities of the current year: Paasche's Price Index = (ΣP1·q1 ÷ ΣP0·q1) × 100. Because it uses the current-year quantities, the weights have to be updated each period (which makes it more cumbersome than Laspeyres', which uses fixed base-year weights). (Paasche's index tends to understate the rise in prices somewhat.) Understanding Paasche's index (current-year quantity weights) is a prelims-relevant point. Paasche's index uses the current-year quantities as weights.

stem: Fisher's 'ideal' index number is the __________ of the Laspeyres and Paasche index numbers.
solution: Fisher's 'ideal' index number is the geometric mean of the Laspeyres index and the Paasche index — i.e., Fisher's Index = √(Laspeyres × Paasche). It is called the 'ideal' index because it combines/balances the two (Laspeyres, which uses base-year weights and tends to overstate, and Paasche, which uses current-year weights and tends to understate), and it satisfies certain desirable mathematical tests (the 'time reversal' and 'factor reversal' tests). So Fisher's ideal index takes the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices, giving a balanced, theoretically superior measure. Understanding that Fisher's index is the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche is a prelims-relevant point. Fisher's ideal index is the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche index numbers.

stem: The process of converting a value at current prices (nominal/money value) into a value at constant prices (real value), by using a price index, is called:
solution: Deflating is the process of converting a value expressed at current prices (a 'nominal' or 'money' value) into a value at constant prices (a 'real' value) — by dividing the nominal value by the price index (and multiplying by 100). This removes the effect of price changes (inflation), so that values from different periods can be compared in 'real' terms. For example, deflating a worker's money wage by the consumer price index gives their 'real wage' (their wage in terms of the goods it can actually buy). Deflating is an important use of price index numbers (converting nominal magnitudes to real ones — e.g., nominal GDP to real GDP, money wages to real wages). Understanding deflating is a prelims-relevant point. Deflating is converting a current-price (nominal/money) value into a constant-price (real) value, using a price index.

stem: The 'real wage' of a worker (the wage adjusted for the price level) is found by dividing the money wage by the __________ (and multiplying by 100).
solution: The 'real wage' of a worker — the wage measured in terms of its actual purchasing power (what the wage can actually buy), adjusted for the price level — is found by dividing the 'money wage' (the nominal wage, in rupees) by the price index (the cost-of-living/consumer price index) and multiplying by 100: Real Wage = (Money Wage ÷ Price Index) × 100. This 'deflates' the money wage to remove the effect of price changes. It is important because a rise in the money wage does not mean a worker is better off if prices have risen just as much (or more) — the real wage (purchasing power) is what matters for the worker's living standard. So the real wage adjusts the money wage for inflation. Understanding the real wage (money wage ÷ price index) is a prelims-relevant point. The real wage is found by dividing the money wage by the price index (and ×100), adjusting the wage for the price level.

stem: If a worker's money wage rises by 10% but prices (the cost of living) rise by 10% as well, the worker's REAL wage:
solution: If a worker's money (nominal) wage rises by 10% but prices (the cost of living) also rise by 10% at the same time, then the worker's real wage stays the same (is unchanged). This is because the real wage measures purchasing power (money wage adjusted for prices): although the worker earns 10% more money, everything now costs 10% more too, so the extra money buys no more goods than before — the worker's purchasing power (real wage) is unchanged. This shows why the real wage (not the money wage) is what matters for a worker's living standard: a money-wage rise that just matches inflation leaves the worker no better off. Understanding this (equal rise in wage and prices → unchanged real wage) is a prelims-relevant point. If the money wage and prices both rise by 10%, the real wage stays the same (purchasing power is unchanged).

stem: The index number used to convert nominal GDP into REAL GDP (adjusting for price changes) is called the GDP:
solution: The GDP deflator is the price index used to convert nominal GDP (GDP measured at current prices) into real GDP (GDP measured at constant/base-year prices) — thereby removing the effect of price changes (inflation) and giving a measure of the actual (real) change in output. Real GDP = (Nominal GDP ÷ GDP deflator) × 100. The GDP deflator is a broad measure of the general price level of all the goods and services included in GDP, and it is itself used as a measure of inflation. So the GDP deflator 'deflates' nominal GDP to real GDP. Understanding the GDP deflator is a prelims-relevant point. The GDP deflator is the price index used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP (adjusting for price changes).

stem: The rate of INFLATION is commonly measured as the percentage change in a __________ from one period to the next.
options: price index (like the CPI or WPI)
solution: The rate of inflation is commonly measured as the percentage change in a price index (such as the Consumer Price Index or the Wholesale Price Index) from one period to the next (e.g., from one year to the next). For example, if the CPI rises from 100 to 106 over a year, the inflation rate for that year is 6% (a 6% rise in the price index). So the inflation rate = the percentage change in the price index. This is why price index numbers (the CPI and WPI) are central to measuring and monitoring inflation. Understanding that inflation is the % change in a price index is a key prelims-relevant point. The rate of inflation is measured as the percentage change in a price index (like the CPI or WPI) from one period to the next.

stem: If the Consumer Price Index rises from 200 to 220 over a year, the rate of inflation for that year is:
solution: The rate of inflation is the percentage change in the price index. Here, the CPI rose from 200 to 220 — an increase of 20 points. The percentage change = (increase ÷ original value) × 100 = (20 ÷ 200) × 100 = 10%. So the rate of inflation for that year is 10%. (Note: it is NOT simply the change of 20 'points' expressed as 20% — inflation is the percentage change relative to the starting value, 200, giving 10%.) Understanding how to calculate the inflation rate from index values (with this example) is a prelims-relevant point. If the CPI rises from 200 to 220, the inflation rate = (20 ÷ 200) × 100 = 10%.

stem: In the Consumer Price Index for a typical household, the item usually given the LARGEST weight (because it takes the biggest share of consumer spending, especially for the poor) is:
solution: In the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for a typical household, the item/group usually given the largest weight is food (and related items) — because food takes the biggest share of consumer spending, especially for poorer households (who spend a large proportion of their income on food). Since the weight of each item reflects its share in the consumer's budget, food (being the biggest expense) gets the largest weight in the index. This means that changes in food prices have the greatest impact on the CPI (and on measured inflation). (Other items — housing, clothing, fuel, transport, etc. — get smaller weights.) Understanding that food gets the largest weight in the CPI is a prelims-relevant point. In the CPI, food usually gets the largest weight, because it takes the biggest share of consumer spending (especially for the poor).

stem: The Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) is especially used to fix/adjust the __________ of workers.
solution: The Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) is a special consumer price index that measures the change in the cost of living of industrial workers. It is especially used to fix and adjust the 'dearness allowance' (DA) of workers (and government employees and pensioners) — the allowance added to their wages/salaries to compensate them for the rise in the cost of living (inflation). When the CPI-IW rises, the DA is increased accordingly, so that workers' real wages/purchasing power are protected against inflation. So the CPI-IW is directly linked to workers' wage adjustments (DA). Understanding this use of the CPI-IW (fixing DA) is a prelims-relevant point. The CPI-IW is especially used to fix/adjust the dearness allowance (DA) of workers, to compensate for the rise in the cost of living.

stem: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI), unlike the Consumer Price Index (CPI), generally does NOT include:
solution: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI), unlike the Consumer Price Index (CPI), generally does NOT include services — the WPI covers only goods/commodities (primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products) traded in the wholesale market, whereas the CPI includes services (like education, health, transport, entertainment) as well as goods, because consumers spend on services too. This is one key difference between the two indices (besides the WPI measuring wholesale/bulk prices and the CPI measuring retail prices paid by consumers). So the WPI is a goods-only wholesale price index. Understanding that the WPI excludes services is a prelims-relevant point. The WPI, unlike the CPI, does not include services — it covers only goods/commodities.

stem: An index number is sometimes described as a 'specialised type of average', because it:
options: summarises/averages the changes in a group of related items (e.g., the prices of many goods) into a single representative figure
solution: An index number is sometimes described as a 'specialised type of average', because — like an average — it summarises the information from a group of related items into a single representative figure. Specifically, an index number averages the relative changes in a group of related variables (for example, the price changes of many different goods) into one single number that represents the overall/general change. So, just as an ordinary average condenses many values into one representative value, an index number condenses many relative changes into one representative measure of change. (It is 'specialised' because it deals with relative changes and can combine items measured in different units, using weights.) Understanding that an index number is a specialised average is a prelims-relevant point. An index number is a specialised type of average, summarising the changes in a group of related items into a single representative figure.

stem: The main problems/difficulties in constructing an index number include selecting the items, choosing the base period, obtaining reliable price data, and:
options: deciding the weights and the method/formula to be used
solution: The main problems/difficulties (decisions to be made) in constructing an index number include: (1) the purpose of the index (what it is for, which guides everything); (2) the selection of the items/commodities to include (choosing a representative basket); (3) the choice of the base period (a normal, suitable period); (4) obtaining reliable, accurate price (or quantity) data (from dependable sources); (5) deciding the weights to assign to the items (reflecting their importance); and (6) choosing the method/formula for constructing the index (simple or weighted, Laspeyres/Paasche/Fisher, etc.). Each of these decisions must be made carefully, as they affect the accuracy and usefulness of the index. So constructing a good index number involves several careful choices. Understanding these problems in construction is a prelims-relevant point. Constructing an index number involves selecting the items, choosing the base period, getting reliable data, and deciding the weights and the method/formula.

stem: The BSE 'Sensex' is a stock market index based on __________ major company stocks, while the NSE 'Nifty' is based on 50.
solution: The BSE Sensex (the Bombay Stock Exchange Sensitive Index) is a stock market index based on 30 major, financially-sound, well-established company stocks (the '30 Sensex companies') traded on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). The NSE Nifty (Nifty 50) is based on 50 major company stocks on the National Stock Exchange (NSE). Both indices track the movements of these representative shares to indicate the overall trend of the stock market (and business sentiment). So: Sensex = 30 stocks (BSE); Nifty = 50 stocks (NSE). Understanding that the Sensex is based on 30 companies (and Nifty on 50) is a prelims-relevant point. The BSE Sensex is based on 30 major company stocks, while the NSE Nifty is based on 50.

stem: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) uses the Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation as the main measure for its policy of __________ (keeping inflation within a target).
solution: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) uses the Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation as the main/target measure of inflation for its monetary policy, under a framework called 'inflation targeting' — in which the RBI aims to keep the CPI inflation rate within a specified target range (with a central target, e.g., 4% with a band of ±2%). Based on how CPI inflation is behaving relative to this target, the RBI adjusts its monetary policy (interest rates, etc.) to control inflation while supporting growth. This shows an important real-world use of a price index number (the CPI) in economic policy. Understanding that the RBI uses CPI inflation for inflation targeting is a prelims-relevant point. The RBI uses CPI inflation as the main measure for its monetary policy of inflation targeting (keeping inflation within a target).

stem: A characteristic feature of index numbers is that they are usually expressed as __________ (percentages relative to the base of 100).
solution: A characteristic feature of index numbers is that they are usually expressed as relatives/percentages — that is, as numbers relative to the base value of 100 (percentages of the base). The base period's value is set at 100, and other periods' values are expressed relative to it (e.g., 120 means 20% above the base, 90 means 10% below). Expressing index numbers in this percentage/relative form (base = 100) makes them easy to understand and to compare, and it allows the combining of items measured in different units. So index numbers are expressed as relatives (percentages of the base). Understanding this characteristic is a prelims-relevant point. Index numbers are usually expressed as relatives/percentages, relative to the base of 100.

stem: The method of constructing index numbers in which each period is compared with the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING period (rather than a fixed base) is the __________ method.
solution: The chain base method is the method of constructing index numbers in which each period's value is compared with (based on) the immediately preceding period — rather than with a single fixed base period (as in the 'fixed base method'). In the chain base method, 'link relatives' are calculated (each period's value as a percentage of the previous period's), and these are then chained/linked together to form the index series. The chain base method is useful when the items or their weights change over time (it allows new items to be introduced), and it shows period-to-period changes; but it is more complex than the fixed base method. Understanding the chain base method is a prelims-relevant point. In the chain base method, each period is compared with the immediately preceding period (using link relatives), rather than a fixed base.

stem: The percentage of a period's value relative to the immediately preceding period's value (used in the chain base method) is called a __________ relative.
solution: A 'link relative' is the value of a period expressed as a percentage of the immediately preceding period's value — i.e., link relative = (current period's value ÷ previous period's value) × 100. Link relatives are the building blocks of the chain base method of constructing index numbers: they show the period-to-period (link-by-link) changes, and they are then 'chained' together (multiplied successively) to obtain the chain index. So a link relative links each period to the one just before it. Understanding the link relative is a prelims-relevant point. A link relative is a period's value expressed as a percentage of the immediately preceding period's value (used in the chain base method).

stem: A rise in the general price level (measured by a price index) means the value of money has __________.
solution: A rise in the general price level (measured by a rising price index) means that the value of money (its purchasing power) has decreased/fallen — because when prices rise, each unit of money buys fewer goods and services (money is worth less). The value of money and the price level are inversely related: higher prices = lower value of money, and lower prices = higher value of money. So inflation (rising prices) erodes the value of money. (This is why the price index is used to measure changes in the value/purchasing power of money and the cost of living.) Understanding this (rising prices → falling value of money) is a prelims-relevant point. A rise in the general price level means the value (purchasing power) of money has decreased.

stem: Index numbers are useful for comparing the cost of living or economic conditions between different __________ as well as over time.
solution: Index numbers are useful for making comparisons not only over time (comparing a value in one period with another — the main use) but also between different places/regions (or between different groups of people). For example, cost-of-living index numbers can be used to compare the cost of living in different cities or regions (to see where it is more expensive to live), or to compare economic conditions (prices, production, etc.) across different areas or groups. So index numbers facilitate comparisons across space (places/groups) as well as across time. Understanding this use (comparison across places, not just time) is a prelims-relevant point. Index numbers are useful for comparing the cost of living or economic conditions between different places/regions as well as over time.

stem: A drawback of the Laspeyres index (which uses fixed base-year weights) is that, over time, the base-year weights become __________ (the consumption pattern changes).
solution: A drawback of the Laspeyres index (which uses fixed base-year quantities/weights) is that, over time, the base-year weights become outdated — less representative of current consumption/production patterns. Because people's consumption patterns change over time (they buy different goods in different proportions as tastes, incomes, and available products change), the base-year weights (fixed from the past) no longer reflect the current pattern of spending, so the index becomes less accurate/representative as time passes. (This is why the base year and weights of an index need to be periodically revised/updated.) So Laspeyres' convenience of fixed weights comes at the cost of the weights becoming outdated. Understanding this drawback is a prelims-relevant point. A drawback of the Laspeyres index is that its fixed base-year weights become outdated over time, as the consumption pattern changes.

stem: The 'base' of an index number is usually revised/updated periodically because:
options: the economy, consumption patterns, and items change over time, so an old base becomes unrepresentative
it is required by law daily
solution: The 'base' of an index number (the base period and the associated weights/basket of items) is usually revised/updated periodically (from time to time) because the economy, the consumption patterns, and the available items/goods change over time — so an old base year and its fixed weights and basket of goods become outdated and unrepresentative of the current situation. For example, new products appear (and old ones vanish), and people's spending patterns shift, so an index based on a very old base (with an old basket and old weights) would no longer accurately measure current changes. Revising the base periodically keeps the index representative and accurate. Understanding why the base is revised periodically is a prelims-relevant point. The base of an index number is revised periodically because the economy, consumption patterns, and items change over time, making an old base unrepresentative.

stem: Which of the following is a use of index numbers in framing government policy?
options: using price indices (like the CPI) to guide monetary policy (controlling inflation) and to adjust wages, pensions, and taxes for inflation
solution: Index numbers are used in framing and guiding government (and central bank) policy in several ways, including: using price indices (like the CPI and WPI) to measure and monitor inflation, which guides monetary policy (the RBI uses CPI inflation for its inflation-targeting policy — adjusting interest rates to control inflation); using the CPI/cost-of-living index to adjust wages, salaries, and pensions for inflation (fixing the dearness allowance) and sometimes to index tax brackets or benefits; using production and trade indices to gauge economic growth and performance and to plan accordingly; and generally using index numbers as 'economic barometers' to understand economic trends and formulate appropriate policies. So index numbers are an important tool in economic policy-making. Understanding this policy-use of index numbers is a prelims-relevant point. Index numbers are used in policy — e.g., price indices (CPI) guide monetary policy against inflation and are used to adjust wages, pensions, and taxes.

stem: A value index number measures the change in the total __________ (price × quantity) of a group of items.
solution: A value index number measures the change over time in the total value of a group of items — where value = price × quantity (i.e., the total amount of money spent or received on the items). So a value index reflects changes in BOTH the prices and the quantities together (the total expenditure/value). For example, a value index of a country's exports would reflect changes in both the prices and the volumes of the exports (their total value). (This contrasts with a price index — measuring only price changes — and a quantity index — measuring only quantity changes.) Understanding the value index number is a prelims-relevant point. A value index number measures the change in the total value (price × quantity) of a group of items.

stem: Which price index is generally more relevant to the common person's cost of living — the CPI or the WPI?
options: both are equally relevant to consumers
solution: The CPI (Consumer Price Index) is generally more relevant to the common person's cost of living than the WPI (Wholesale Price Index). This is because the CPI measures the change in the RETAIL prices of the goods AND services that consumers actually buy (the prices they pay in the market) — so it directly reflects the cost of living and the inflation experienced by ordinary consumers/households. The WPI, by contrast, measures wholesale (bulk) prices of goods only (excluding services), which are the prices at an earlier stage of trade, not the retail prices consumers pay. So, for measuring the common person's cost of living and retail inflation, the CPI is the more relevant index. (This is also why the RBI uses CPI inflation as its policy target.) Understanding that the CPI is more relevant to consumers' cost of living is a prelims-relevant point. The CPI (Consumer Price Index) is more relevant to the common person's cost of living, as it measures the retail prices of goods and services consumers actually buy.

stem: Assertion (A): The Consumer Price Index is used to adjust the wages/salaries of workers over time. Reason (R): As prices rise (the CPI increases), workers need higher money wages to maintain the same real purchasing power / standard of living. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) is used to adjust the wages/salaries of workers over time (e.g., through the dearness allowance). And the reason is (R) that as prices rise (the CPI increases), the purchasing power of a fixed money wage falls, so workers need higher money wages just to maintain the same real purchasing power / standard of living as before. Because the CPI measures exactly this rise in the cost of living, it is used to work out how much to raise the workers' wages to compensate for the price rise (so their real wages are protected). So R correctly explains why the CPI is used to adjust wages (A). Understanding this (CPI adjusts wages to protect real purchasing power against rising prices) is a prelims-relevant point. The CPI is used to adjust workers' wages because, as prices rise (CPI up), workers need higher money wages to maintain the same real purchasing power.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Index Numbers' is that:
options: An index number is a statistical device that measures the relative change in a variable (or a group of variables) — such as prices (the CPI and WPI), quantity/production (the IIP), or share values (the Sensex) — over time, relative to a base period (taken as 100); index numbers (which use weights for importance and a normal base period) are vital 'economic barometers' for measuring inflation, adjusting wages, and studying and comparing economic conditions, though they give only an approximate/general measure
Index numbers measure only the weather
Only one price can be tracked
solution: The chapter conveys that an index number is a statistical device/measure that shows the relative change (percentage change) in a variable — or, more usefully, in a group of related variables — over time, by comparing the current period with a chosen base period (whose value is taken as 100). It explains the key terms: the base period (the reference period, = 100, which should be a normal, not abnormal, period) and the current/given period (the period being compared), and how to read an index (e.g., an index of 120 means a 20% rise since the base). It describes the main types of index numbers: price index numbers (measuring changes in the price level) — most importantly the Consumer Price Index (CPI, the cost-of-living index, measuring retail prices paid by consumers, used to gauge inflation and adjust wages/pensions/dearness allowance) and the Wholesale Price Index (WPI, measuring wholesale prices); quantity/volume index numbers (measuring changes in physical output/quantities) — like the Index of Industrial Production (IIP); and value indices and others (like the stock market indices — Sensex/Nifty — tracking share prices). It notes the importance of using weights (to reflect the relative importance of different items — a weighted index being more accurate than a simple one) and a proper (normal) base period, and it highlights the many uses of index numbers — as 'economic barometers' that indicate economic trends — for measuring inflation and the changing purchasing power of money (which falls as prices rise), adjusting wages and pensions, comparing economic conditions over time and across places, and framing economic policy. It also cautions that index numbers give only an approximate, general (average) measure of change, which may not apply exactly to every individual item or person. Understanding what index numbers are, their base/current periods, the main types (price — CPI, WPI; quantity — IIP; etc.), the role of weights, their uses as economic barometers, and their limitations is the central concern of this chapter. An index number measures the relative change in a variable (like prices, production, or share values) over time relative to a base of 100 — a vital 'economic barometer' (CPI, WPI, IIP, etc.) for measuring inflation, adjusting wages, and comparing economic conditions, though it gives only an approximate, general measure.
